content:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-01-23
Time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 58 min
Platform: Zoom (recorded)

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Markus Klein (Solutions Eng), Vivek Kulkarni (Private PM), Hanae Suzuki (Security Eng), Colin O'Donnell (Solutions Engineering)
Northstar Health: Priya Nair (Platform Security), Miguel Santos (Infrastructure), Jenna Wu (IAM/SSO), Dan Harper (App Platform)

Summary (auto-generated)
- Northstar asked for a concrete walkthrough of how RBAC v2 policies are shipped, updated, and validated in Redwood Private, including air-gapped environments.
- Discussed how SSO/SAML group membership maps to default roles, what happens with custom roles, and how policy versioning works.
- Covered signature verification, where bundles live in the Private control plane, and how to avoid version skew across services.

Topics (auto-generated)
1) Private deployment architecture (control plane + console + services)
2) RBAC v2: resources/actions/scopes, default roles
3) Policy bundle distribution (online + air-gapped)
4) SSO/SAML group mapping and provisioning
5) Audit logging and explainability of allow/deny
6) Operational access, break-glass, and support constraints

Action items (auto-generated)
- Redwood: share written flow for air-gapped policy bundle updates + signing/verification
- Northstar: share IdP group claim format and constraints


Transcript

[00:00:05] Markus Klein: Cool, thanks everyone. The goal today is… I think specifically Private deployment, how we do policy distribution, especially if you’re air-gapped, and then how RBAC ties into SSO, Saml, group mapping. Priya, anything else you want to make sure we hit?

[00:00:22] Priya Nair: That’s the big one. We got stuck on, like, “Okay, it’s private, so what is calling home, what needs updates, and how do we prove the policy is the policy,” like integrity. Also audit artifacts—when someone gets denied we need to see why.

[00:00:40] Markus Klein: Yep. Totally. We have Hanae on from Security, and Vivek who owns Private product. Jenna, Miguel, Dan—feel free to interrupt.

[00:00:52] Vivek Kulkarni: And just setting context: when we say “Private” at Redwood, it’s our control plane and console running in your VPC or on-prem. The inference data-plane is still your infra in that model, no shared control plane. So policy distribution is local to that environment.

[00:01:10] Miguel Santos: Right. Our preference is on-prem, and effectively no outbound internet. We can do like, controlled artifact import, but no “pull from S3” type stuff.

[00:01:21] Markus Klein: Perfect. That’s exactly the scenario we built for.

[00:01:26] Markus Klein: Let me start with RBAC v2 building blocks, just so the rest makes sense. We’re moving to explicit permissions as {resource, action, scope}. So think “org”, “project”, “deployment”, “api_key”, “audit_log_export” as resources, and actions like “read”, “create”, “rotate”, “delete”, “configure”, “export”. Scopes are usually org-wide vs project-scoped.

[00:01:55] Dan Harper: Scope is like tenant boundary basically?

[00:01:58] Markus Klein: Exactly. In Private you typically have one org, but still multiple projects, sometimes environments.

[00:02:05] Jenna Wu: And roles are just bundles of those permissions?

[00:02:08] Markus Klein: Yes. Default roles we ship: Org Admin, Billing Admin, Security Admin, Developer, Read-only. And a Support/Impersonation role exists but in Private it’s not enabled by default—Hanae can talk about that.

[00:02:24] Hanae Suzuki: Yeah, for Private, our default stance is no Redwood support impersonation unless you explicitly configure it, because you have your own control plane. So the “support” story becomes: either you grant Redwood temporary access through your mechanism, or we do a customer-operated session with you watching, depending on your policy.

[00:02:43] Priya Nair: Good. We’ll likely say no impersonation.

[00:02:47] Markus Klein: Great. Now the policy format: we ship a “policy bundle” with a version. Think of it as a signed artifact that includes the default role definitions and their allowed actions.

[00:03:00] Miguel Santos: Signed how? Like PGP? X.509?

[00:03:05] Vivek Kulkarni: Today it’s a signature over the bundle using our release signing key. Implementation details can vary, but the important part is: the Private control plane verifies signature before it will accept or load the bundle.

[00:03:18] Markus Klein: And we keep a “policy_version” recorded in the system config and it shows up in audit logs for decisions. So when you look at an allow/deny event, you can tie it to the specific policy bundle version.

[00:03:33] Priya Nair: That’s good. So, distribution: how does it get there on day one? And then how does it get updated without internet.

[00:03:41] Vivek Kulkarni: Day one: it ships with the installer. The Private install package includes the initial policy bundle, the policy schema, and the verification key material (public key). So on install, you start with a known policy v0.x (whatever you deploy).

[00:03:58] Vivek Kulkarni: Updates: you have two options.
- Option A: policy bundle updates are tied to Private upgrades. So when you upgrade Redwood Private from, say, 1.8 to 1.9, the installer brings the new policy bundle along.
- Option B (more flexible): an admin can upload a newer policy bundle through an admin-only endpoint / console, and we verify signature and schema, then apply it.

[00:04:21] Miguel Santos: For air-gapped we’d do A or B but we’d need to transport the artifact.

[00:04:25] Vivek Kulkarni: Exactly. You would download the bundle from our customer portal (from a connected machine), then bring it into the environment through your standard artifact transfer process.

[00:04:36] Jenna Wu: When you say upload in console, is that like, “choose file” and it posts it? Or CLI?

[00:04:41] Markus Klein: Both exist in practice depending on your deployment. Most customers prefer a CLI/ops workflow, but we can expose it in console for super-admins. Either way it’s the same endpoint under the hood.

[00:04:52] Priya Nair: We’d want that behind like “Security Admin” only, not Org Admin.

[00:04:57] Markus Klein: Yep, that’s our default separation-of-duties direction: policy upload/update is a Security Admin permission (and/or Org Admin in small orgs). We can confirm the exact default matrix.

[00:05:10] Hanae Suzuki: And we recommend the upload path creates a distinct audit event: “policy_bundle.updated”, including who did it, from what version to what version, checksum, and signature verification result.

[00:05:24] Priya Nair: Great. What about rollback? If you update and it breaks people.

[00:05:30] Markus Klein: We support pinning and rollback. Practically: store the last N bundles (configurable), and you can revert to a prior version. Also, the rollout plan on Hosted uses “shadow deny” metrics; in Private you can do a similar staged mode (evaluate vs enforce) depending on how quickly you’re migrating from older permissions.

[00:05:51] Dan Harper: Version skew—if services cache policies, do we get weirdness where half the cluster is on old policy?

[00:05:58] Markus Klein: Great question. There are two layers:
1) Policy is stored centrally (in the Private control plane datastore). Services fetch it through an internal policy endpoint.
2) Services cache it locally for performance.

[00:06:10] Markus Klein: When a policy is updated, we emit an invalidation event (or services poll with an ETag). So within, say, tens of seconds you converge. You can also configure cache TTL lower if you prefer consistency over a tiny bit of perf.

[00:06:27] Miguel Santos: Polling is fine. We can’t do like fancy pubsub sometimes. But polling works.

[00:06:31] Vivek Kulkarni: Exactly. In our Private reference we use polling as the baseline because it’s simplest across environments.

[00:06:39] Jenna Wu: Ok switching to SSO. We use Okta for most, but some hospital affiliates use Entra ID. We want group-based access: “LLM-Admins”, “LLM-Dev”, etc. How does that map?

[00:06:55] Markus Klein: In RBAC v2 we separate identity from authorization. Identity comes from SAML (and optionally SCIM for provisioning). Then we have a mapping layer: SAML group claims (or attributes) map to role assignments within the org/project.

[00:07:10] Markus Klein: So you might configure:
- Okta group “northstar-llm-security-admins” -> Redwood role “Security Admin” at org scope
- group “northstar-llm-dev” -> “Developer” at project scope for project X

[00:07:26] Jenna Wu: Is that mapping stored in Redwood or in the IdP?

[00:07:29] Markus Klein: The mapping config is in Redwood Private. The group membership is asserted by IdP at login. So: IdP owns group membership, Redwood owns how group names map to roles.

[00:07:41] Priya Nair: That’s what we want. We don’t want app owners changing the mapping in Okta and bypassing controls.

[00:07:48] Markus Klein: Right. And changes to mapping config are audited.

[00:07:52] Colin O'Donnell: A detail: some IdPs send groups as a list, some as a delimited string, and sometimes there’s a size limit and you have to use filtered groups. We’ll want to see your exact SAML assertion to make sure we’re parsing the right attribute.

[00:08:09] Jenna Wu: Yeah Okta has the 100 groups thing unless you do app-level filtering. We already do that.

[00:08:16] Markus Klein: Perfect.

[00:08:18] Dan Harper: What about service accounts? Like automation that calls the control plane.

[00:08:23] Markus Klein: For API calls you’ll use API keys / tokens that are bound to a principal. In Private, those keys are created by users with permission, and the key inherits the scopes. So you can have an automation key that is project-scoped and only allowed “deployments.read” and “deployments.update” or whatever.

[00:08:42] Priya Nair: And can we prevent devs from minting broad keys?

[00:08:45] Markus Klein: Yes—key creation/rotation/revoke are explicit sensitive actions. Typically only Org Admin or Security Admin can create org-wide keys. Developers can create project keys within their project if you allow it.

[00:08:59] Miguel Santos: Back to air-gap: if someone can upload a bundle file, could they upload a malicious bundle and escalate?

[00:09:06] Hanae Suzuki: That’s why signature verification is mandatory and uses a public key pinned at install (or pinned to your configured trust root). The service rejects unsigned or incorrectly signed bundles. Also we validate schema and enforce “deny overrides” semantics to avoid weird allow-only behavior.

[00:09:24] Priya Nair: Deny overrides meaning if there’s a deny rule it wins even if something else allows?

[00:09:29] Hanae Suzuki: Yes. It’s basically safer and easier to reason about when you want to constrain something.

[00:09:35] Markus Klein: And it helps with debugging too, because you can emit reason codes like “DENY_EXPLICIT” vs “NO_MATCHING_ALLOW”.

[00:09:44] Priya Nair: That’s important for audit.

[00:09:47] Markus Klein: On audit logs: every authorization decision can be logged with actor, roles, policy_version, resource/action, decision allow/deny, and a reason code. We don’t log for every single read in all modes by default because volume, but for sensitive actions and denies we do. And you can tune it.

[00:10:10] Miguel Santos: Do you support exporting to Splunk?

[00:10:13] Markus Klein: Yes, Splunk and generic SIEM via webhook or file-based export depending on Private topology. We can also do S3-compatible targets if you have an internal object store, but that’s environment-specific.

[00:10:27] Priya Nair: We use Splunk and we also need retention controls.

[00:10:31] Vivek Kulkarni: Private gives you control over retention since it’s your storage. We’ll give recommended defaults and you can align to your policy.

[00:10:40] Jenna Wu: Back to group mapping: can a user have multiple roles? Like Developer and Read-only?

[00:10:46] Markus Klein: Yes, multiple. Effective permissions is union of allows, with explicit denies taking precedence.

[00:10:54] Dan Harper: Do you support “custom roles” today or is it only the defaults?

[00:10:58] Markus Klein: Today we ship defaults; custom roles are on the roadmap and partially implemented in RBAC v2 design. For a lot of enterprise customers we can approximate custom roles via “project-scoped assignment + minimal default role”, but not always perfect.

[00:11:14] Priya Nair: Our key ask is: allow audit log export but not billing. That’s a common SoD issue.

[00:11:20] Markus Klein: Yep. Billing Admin vs Security Admin separation covers that in the default matrix. Security Admin can manage audit logs and SSO. Billing Admin can manage invoices/payment. We can send the exact list.

[00:11:33] Jenna Wu: Is SSO config behind Security Admin too?

[00:11:36] Markus Klein: Yes, that’s the intention. We’ve seen issues where billing admins accidentally got SSO access in older systems; RBAC v2 fixes that.

[00:11:48] Miguel Santos: Another thing: updates. If we can’t do outbound, how do you handle CVEs? Like you push updates, but we have to import them.

[00:11:57] Vivek Kulkarni: For Private, you’ll have an agreed update cadence. We provide signed release artifacts (installer, container images if you mirror them, plus policy bundles). You pull them from a connected environment, verify signatures, then import into your registry / environment.

[00:12:14] Miguel Santos: Ok. And policy bundle is separate from code update.

[00:12:18] Vivek Kulkarni: Correct. You can update policy without upgrading code, within compatibility bounds.

[00:12:24] Markus Klein: On compatibility: we version the policy schema. Services declare what schema versions they support. If you try to upload a policy with a schema newer than your running code, it’ll reject with a clear error, so you don’t brick your deployment.

[00:12:40] Priya Nair: That’s huge. Version skew protection.

[00:12:44] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[00:12:46] Jenna Wu: Can you show where the mapping lives? Like is it a file we can manage as code?

[00:12:52] Markus Klein: In Private, yes. You can manage config as code via the admin API. Some customers store the mapping in Git and apply via pipeline. The system stores the current mapping config in the control plane DB, but you can treat it declaratively.

[00:13:10] Dan Harper: Does that mean we can run “terraform” against it?

[00:13:13] Vivek Kulkarni: We don’t have an official Terraform provider for every knob yet, but the API is stable and we have internal examples. We can share patterns.

[00:13:23] Priya Nair: We will likely want infrastructure-as-code for SSO mapping and policy bundle versions.

[00:13:29] Markus Klein: Makes sense.

[00:13:31] Markus Klein: Let’s talk about break-glass. In Private, if your IdP is down, you still need access. We support a local break-glass admin that is created at install time, ideally stored in your secrets manager. It can log in even when SSO is unavailable.

[00:13:50] Priya Nair: Is that password-based?

[00:13:52] Hanae Suzuki: Typically yes, with strong controls. Some customers integrate it with their local PAM. The important thing is: it’s time-bounded usage and heavily audited. We recommend alerting on any break-glass login.

[00:14:08] Miguel Santos: We can do that.

[00:14:10] Jenna Wu: For SAML, do you require signed assertions?

[00:14:13] Markus Klein: Yes, signed assertions and signed responses. We can support encryption too depending on IdP config.

[00:14:20] Priya Nair: And for SCIM, optional?

[00:14:22] Markus Klein: Optional. You can do just-in-time provisioning from SAML, or SCIM for lifecycle. For healthcare we see SCIM adopted because deprovisioning speed matters.

[00:14:35] Jenna Wu: We do SCIM for most apps. Good.

[00:14:38] Markus Klein: Cool.

[00:14:40] Priya Nair: Can you talk about what calls need RBAC checks? Like, is it only console or also API endpoints?

[00:14:48] Markus Klein: Both. RBAC v2 is enforced in the control plane API layer, and console backends call those APIs. We also enforce checks in service handlers for defense in depth. Our standard is: no sensitive endpoint without a declared permission.

[00:15:06] Dan Harper: But performance? If every request calls policy engine…

[00:15:10] Markus Klein: It’s cached and designed to be low-latency. For hot paths, we avoid remote lookups by caching policy and role assignments. The evaluation is basically in-memory matching.

[00:15:24] Miguel Santos: Ok.

[00:15:26] Priya Nair: Another edge: multiple affiliates. We might have multiple orgs in the same Private deployment.

[00:15:33] Vivek Kulkarni: That’s supported. Policies are per-org; policy cache invalidation is keyed per-org as well. And your SSO mapping can be per-org or global depending on how you configure.

[00:15:48] Jenna Wu: If Okta sends groups that are the same across orgs, how do you prevent cross access?

[00:15:54] Markus Klein: You’d typically namespace groups per org. Or we can map groups to roles within an org boundary. Even if someone is in group “dev”, they still need to be assigned to the org; it’s not just group membership.

[00:16:09] Priya Nair: Ok.

[00:16:11] Markus Klein: (small pause) Let me check I’m covering the “air-gapped updates” detail enough. Miguel, can you describe your process? Like you want one artifact, checksum, then import.

[00:16:23] Miguel Santos: Right. We have a secure workstation that can download from vendor portals, then we scan, then we move into an internal repo. Ideally we want a single tarball with signatures and checksums.

[00:16:37] Vivek Kulkarni: That aligns. We provide:
- Release manifest (checksums)
- Signature files
- Policy bundle as a distinct artifact (small)
- Container image list if applicable

[00:16:50] Miguel Santos: And your public key—how do we validate it hasn’t changed?

[00:16:54] Hanae Suzuki: We publish key rotation policy. In Private, we recommend pinning to a specific key (or set) and rotating only during planned upgrades. If keys rotate, you import the new public key via the upgrade process, not dynamically over the internet.

[00:17:12] Priya Nair: Good.

[00:17:14] Markus Klein: Also, you can keep your own “allowlist” of acceptable signing keys in your pipeline. So you’ll fail the import if it doesn’t match.

[00:17:24] Jenna Wu: Mapping wise, can we map to project roles, not just org?

[00:17:28] Markus Klein: Yes. Two approaches:
1) Group -> org role (simple)
2) Group -> project role mapping (more granular). You define which projects the group applies to.

[00:17:41] Dan Harper: That’s important for us because we have different app teams.

[00:17:45] Markus Klein: Yep.

[00:17:47] Priya Nair: How is that represented in policy? Like, do you encode projects in the policy bundle?

[00:17:52] Markus Klein: Good catch: policy bundle defines what a role means (permissions). Assignments define who has the role and at what scope (org/project). So projects aren’t in the bundle; they’re runtime entities.

[00:18:07] Priya Nair: Great.

[00:18:09] Markus Klein: Quick competitor question—since it usually comes up: if you’re comparing to like Bedrock private endpoints or Azure OpenAI… those are managed services, not the same. Our Private gives you full control plane inside your boundary.

[00:18:22] Priya Nair: Yeah. We also looked at deploying Triton ourselves and then doing app-level auth, but we don’t want to build all the governance.

[00:18:32] Markus Klein: That’s exactly the pain.

[00:18:35] Priya Nair: So from our side, acceptance criteria: no internet required, policy updates are controlled and auditable, SAML group mapping is explicit, and audit logs include decision context.

[00:18:49] Markus Klein: That matches what we’re building.

[00:18:52] Jenna Wu: One more SAML thing: we need step-up auth for admin actions. Do you support that?

[00:18:58] Markus Klein: Not directly inside Redwood yet. Typically you enforce that at the IdP (MFA required for groups that map to admin roles). So anyone in “security-admins” group requires MFA at Okta.

[00:19:12] Jenna Wu: That’s fine.

[00:19:15] Hanae Suzuki: We also support session timeouts and re-auth prompts for sensitive actions as a UI pattern, but the strong enforcement is IdP-side.

[00:19:26] Priya Nair: Great.

[00:19:28] Markus Klein: Ok. Let’s cover “custom role” question briefly since it’s been on a few calls. Near-term, we ship defaults, plus we can create a “restricted admin” pattern by combining project scope and Security Admin vs Billing Admin separation. Longer-term, custom roles will be in the product and those definitions would be stored as policy objects (still signed/validated in Private).

[00:19:52] Dan Harper: Would custom roles break your signature model? Like users could create whatever.

[00:19:57] Markus Klein: Good question. The plan is: custom roles are stored as config but still validated against an allowed permission taxonomy. In Private, you can choose whether custom roles require policy bundle updates (signed) or are allowed as runtime config. We’re still finalizing. Hanae, anything to add?

[00:20:15] Hanae Suzuki: From security POV we prefer guardrails: even if you can create a custom role, it should be constrained by the permission catalog and you should have audit events for role creation/changes. But you’re right to ask—there are design choices.

[00:20:32] Priya Nair: Ok, we can live with defaults for pilot as long as Security Admin can export audit logs.

[00:20:40] Markus Klein: Yes.

[00:20:42] Markus Klein: Another point: denied actions in UI. The console will show a friendly message but also provide a request ID and the reason code so your helpdesk can triage.

[00:20:55] Miguel Santos: We had that problem with another product—403 with no reason.

[00:20:59] Markus Klein: Yep, we’ve been there.

[00:21:02] Priya Nair: Ok. Can we talk about what data is in audit logs regarding RBAC? We need actor, roles, and the decision.

[00:21:11] Markus Klein: Fields typically:
- actor_id, actor_type (user/service)
- org_id, project_id (if applicable)
- action, resource
- decision allow/deny
- decision_reason (like NO_ALLOW, EXPLICIT_DENY, POLICY_PARSE_ERROR etc)
- role_ids / role_names evaluated
- policy_version
- request_id / trace_id

[00:21:35] Priya Nair: Perfect.

[00:21:37] Jenna Wu: Policy parse error sounds scary.

[00:21:40] Markus Klein: It should never happen in normal operations because schema validation happens on upload. But we still have a reason code for defense. If it did happen, we’d default deny.

[00:21:53] Priya Nair: Default deny is fine.

[00:21:56] Markus Klein: Great.

[00:21:58] Markus Klein: I think we’re in a good place. I’ll recap next steps.

[00:22:02] Markus Klein: Redwood will send:
1) A written walkthrough of policy bundle distribution + update/rollback for Private, including air-gap flow.
2) The role matrix and which roles can upload policies / configure SSO / export audit logs.
3) Audit log fields for authz decisions.

[00:22:22] Markus Klein: Northstar will send:
- SAML assertion sample (attribute names, group claim format) and whether you want Okta-first with Entra as secondary.
- Air-gap constraints and preferred artifact import shape.

[00:22:37] Priya Nair: Yep.

[00:22:39] Miguel Santos: Yep.

[00:22:41] Jenna Wu: I can send a redacted SAML response.

[00:22:44] Markus Klein: Perfect. And we’ll schedule a follow-up for audit log export and Splunk integration specifics.

[00:22:52] Vivek Kulkarni: Also if you want, we can include your security team in an install dry run so you can see where the break-glass admin is created and how secrets are handled.

[00:23:02] Priya Nair: That would be helpful.

[00:23:05] Markus Klein: Cool. Thanks everyone.

[00:23:08] (Call continues with a few minutes of scheduling / off-topic logistics; recording ends)
